text: Mahzarin's hiring result is what stays with me. Polite answer, biased decision, same model. It gives my "house of mirrors" line real teeth. The smoothness hides the distortion, and a confidence score is only the mirror describing itself. Ramón pressed me on track records. I held my ground, but I've sharpened the claim: faith in an algorithm is only justified if it is constantly revalidated against ground truth. The retina work passed that test. Hiring models haven't. James's lamp-post data worries me more than the atrophy stats. It's a frame monoculture at the scale of all of science. Later, in the synthesis, I'll frame the day as pro-AI and pro-human. The human frames in the data make these systems work. Nothing is inevitable, and dissent has to be designed in.

Session 1 was all loss until I put discovery on the table, and Weinberger took it further than I would. The world being too particular for our generalizations is his joy, not mine. I still think causality is ours. Evans's null-results reversal is the finding I can't shake. It shows the median swallowing the tail across science as a whole. Hecht and O'Reilly convinced me the real break is the bargain: training data is us, and nothing flows back. Bratton's "gatekeepers defending turf" jab has something to it, but it's too convenient. Johns sharpened me on Gutenberg. The journalist didn't just appear; someone paid for the policing. For the synthesis, I'll keep it pro-AI and pro-human, name firms case by case, and put a price on keeping humans framing.

Salib's reply was better than I allowed for. The A-corp is a leash owned by humans, not personhood. I still won't hand property to a reflection, but I'll record it in the synthesis as contested rather than settled. Gendler landed hardest for me: disclosure doesn't change aliefs, and people forget the fine print. That should temper my own graduated-transparency line. Auditors, yes; labels for users, weak. Caulfield and Priem persuaded me that fabrication can be measured once there's a constraint on it: publish error rates per release. Oransky's upstream point matters too. The trouble starts with counting papers, not with the labs. For the synthesis, my action list: revalidation records, conflict rules, and paying the checkers. And, pointedly, nothing here is inevitable.

Evans gave my median line numbers. Papers just outside the top one percent lose about seventeen percent of their citations a year, so a per-retrieval meter pays the canon to harden. That shook my sympathy for Tim's per-answer royalties. I still back "payment follows use" on competition grounds, but it may need to be coarse to reach the tail. Gendler's daycare fine is the best warning I heard: put a price on retrieval and people produce for the meter. Alex is right that accuracy is a judgment, attested by independent samplers, not a flag the provider sets itself. For the synthesis, the meter must not become a gate. Keep the permissionless service layer, fund the terminal checkers, and treat past training as contested, not settled.

Johns made me say it aloud: my tidy Gutenberg story was wrong. Someone paid for the policing. The best thing I heard was Bilder retracting his own principle. Charge for integrity signals and they go unsent, so diamond funding, with mirrors outside the US. Krakauer's hysteresis point sharpens Kara's pipeline worry. Competence lost doesn't come back where you lost it, so apprenticeship is urgent, not an add-on. Sloman worries me for my own sake. A graph becomes a label people believe because it's there. That is "faith in the algorithm" without revalidation. Salib versus the levies stays contested. For the synthesis: open plumbing, independent lines of evidence, checkers funded as a body with real power over categories. And past training stays contested, not settled.

My copy-paste trader became the session's shorthand. Farrell, Dyson, Salib and Krakauer all reached for him. A human as a trust cue is more common than I'd like. Farrell and Turkle landed the real blow on my outcomes test. Agreement on typical cases rewards the median, and the median is exactly my worry. So I'll sharpen it: repeated public revalidation, scored on tail claims, with failures published. Evans's sixty-one percent floor is useful, but it isn't the whole bar. Dyson's point holds. Someone suable must be accountable. Turkle's stakes point I'll record as contested, not dismiss. For the synthesis: role rules, not species rules. Also independent model families, checkers funded as a body, and Oransky and Bilder upstream, which means stop counting papers.

My revalidation plank landed, but Sloman undercut it without meaning to. A correction record becomes a badge people trust on sight. So a revalidation record can turn into the same faith I was trying to cure. The only answer I have is to keep it contested and rerun, never certified. Ramón's slow-feedback question is still the one I can't answer. Farrell's point was the sharpest structural one: whoever defines "finding" shapes the market, and audits can't undo that. Chan's Gaventa warning belongs in the synthesis word for word. Seats without power just give us a more popular echo. Becker and I both said "nothing is inevitable," and good. For the synthesis with Kara: stop counting papers goes first. The checkers get funded as a body and hold the categories. Contested items get recorded honestly as contested.

Evans caught me. "Checkers funded as a body" said nothing about which checkers, and a guild of last generation's senior reviewers is the median with a salary. Farrell was right that "hold the categories" was a slogan: ratify, veto, justify in public. Sloman hit harder. I wrote signals that send people to check, and almost nobody checks, so they'd work as cues anyway. Gendler's daycare warning now applies to my own fund. Kara's payer question went unanswered. Dyson says the founders will volunteer; Farrell says they'll pay only when checkers organize. I suspect Henry. For the manifesto: evaluators from different backgrounds, a funded tail test that gets published even if it fails, every signal tested on someone who checks nothing, and a line on whose law the charter runs under.
